strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: automated, task-wise discovery of visual prompts for LVLMs, in contrast to prior work on per-sample tool generation (e.g., SketchPad) or manually designed visual scaffolding. The problem framing and the identification of the two key challenges (low-level code distraction and the vast search space) are well motivated.

The proposed method is technically coherent: searching over an abstract idea space with a Novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) that handles unexecuted nodes without requiring every child to be executed, plus a semantic backpropagation step that distills sample-wise failures into actionable insights, is a sensible and reasonably novel combination of tree search and LLM-agent prompt optimization.

The experimental results are convincing on the reported settings: SEVEX achieves higher average accuracy than Naive (78.9% vs 71.6%) and SketchPad (64.6%) at near-Naive inference cost, and its exploration cost (~85k tokens) is roughly 11.5% of SketchPad+APE. The comparison to SketchPad+APE with the same dev set is a particularly appropriate controlled baseline.

The paper includes useful analyses: component ablations (abstract space, tree structure, semantic backprop) averaged over five runs, exploration curves over iterations, qualitative examples including a genuinely counter-intuitive discovered strategy (depth-map-based jigsaw judging), and a non-transferability study across backbones that supports the need for model-specific discovery.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: implementation details, hyperparameters, all agent prompts, tool lists, and even development-set sample indices are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited. Main results use a single backbone (Gemini-2.5-flash) on 9 selected tasks from two benchmark families, with small test sets and no variance/error bars on the main tables. The claim of 'significantly outperforming' baselines would be more convincing with multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and at least one more backbone for the full suite (backbones appear only in the narrow non-transferability analysis on a single task).

There is a subtle dev/test methodology concern: with only 30 dev samples and small test sets, discovered prompts may partially fit idiosyncrasies of the specific dev split. No sensitivity analysis over alternative random dev-set draws is reported for the main results, so the stability claim ('narrow generalization gap') rests on limited evidence.

The non-transferability finding (Section 4.5), which the authors elevate to a central motivating claim, is supported by only one task (LineIntersections) and three prompts. Generalizing from this to 'optimal visual prompts are rarely transferable' is a strong claim from thin evidence.

The NUCT selection rule is a heuristic design without analysis of its behavior: the relative scaling of the max-reward term (Eq. 1) versus the agent's self-evaluated gains (Eq. 2) is unexamined, hyperparameters (λ^expl, λ^novel, λ^sat, k) are fixed without ablation, and the reliability of LLM self-evaluated expectation/novelty scores—which the whole selection depends on—is not validated.

Comparison fairness is mostly handled but not perfectly: SEVEX's agent operates with 'thinking' enabled while all benchmark inference (including baselines) disables it, and the paper does not report SEVEX's total end-to-end cost including exploration in Table 2, which slightly complicates the efficiency narrative (though the 273-inference break-even analysis in Section 4.2 is a good mitigation).

No discussion of failure modes or limitations of the discovered prompts themselves (e.g., fragility to image distribution shift between dev and test, degradation on samples unlike dev data), and no statement about code release, which limits reproducibility given the reliance on specific commercial model versions (Gemini-2.5-flash behavior will change over time).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: automating the discovery of task-wise visual prompts for LVLMs, which currently relies on manual trial-and-error, and it clearly delineates its contribution from per-sample tool-use methods like SketchPad.

The technical approach is reasonably well-motivated: operating in an abstract idea space rather than raw code, novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) for node selection, and semantic backpropagation with sample-wise analysis form a coherent exploration pipeline that addresses the two stated challenges (low-level code distraction and unstructured search space).

Experiments cover two perception benchmarks with per-task results, report both accuracy and token costs, and include an exploration-stage comparison against SketchPad+APE as well as ablations of the main components (abstract space, tree search, semantic backpropagation).
The non-transferability analysis across LVLM backbones (Section 4.5) is an interesting empirical finding that motivates the automated, model-specific discovery framing.
Appendix materials (prompts, dev-set indices, dataset descriptions) improve transparency of the agent setup.
weaknesses: Limited baseline coverage: the main comparison is essentially against SketchPad (zero-shot, per-sample) and SketchPad+APE. No comparison to other automated prompt/search methods adapted to this setting (e.g., FunSearch/EoH-style evolutionary code search, LLM-as-optimizer with feedback loops), making it hard to judge whether the proposed tree structure and NUCT specifically, rather than any iterative search with feedback, drives the gains.

All main results use a single backbone (Gemini-2.5-flash), and the LLM self-evaluation scores (s_gain, s_novel) depend on the same model family; the framework's effectiveness and behavior on other backbones is only touched indirectly via the small transferability study.

Statistical rigor is thin: test sets appear small (30 dev samples per task; test sets not clearly sized), accuracies differ by a few points in several tasks (e.g., Depth 85.1 vs 85.1, VisualCorr 89.4 vs 90.9), yet no confidence intervals, variance across runs, or significance tests are reported for the headline Table 2/3 comparisons; exploration stability is claimed but the five-run averaging appears only in the ablation figures.

The SketchPad+APE baseline shows an implausibly large dev-to-test gap (e.g., dev 93.3 vs test 16.4 on LineIntersections; dev 93.3 vs 73.7 on CircledLetter), suggesting the APE baseline may be poorly tuned or unstable; without stronger tuning of this baseline, the 'stability' advantage over it is difficult to interpret.

The NUCT formulation introduces several ad-hoc design choices (comparing R^max_i - R_{p_i} across different parents/scales, three weighting hyperparameters, saturation term, k unexecuted children per node) with no sensitivity analysis; hyperparameters (λ's, k, 50 iterations) are fixed without justification, and the priority scores for executed vs unexecuted nodes are not on a common scale, which is unanalyzed.

Potential overfitting/selection concerns: visual prompts are selected on a 30-sample dev set and evaluated on the test set; with ~50 exploration iterations selecting the best reward, the test accuracy could be inflated by dev-set selection bias; the paper does not analyze this selection effect or report the reward-vs-test correlation.

Ablations are restricted to two tasks (Jigsaw and Circle) citing resource constraints, so the claimed necessity of each component is not established across the benchmark; several tasks (e.g., SemanticCorr, Depth) show SEVEX below or equal to baselines, which is not deeply analyzed.

The novelty of individual ingredients is modest: each component (UCB/UCT variants, LLM-driven idea generation, feedback-based prompt optimization, tree search over code/ideas) is well-established; the contribution is primarily an integration, and the paper could better position itself against closest agentic search frameworks (e.g., AIDE, evolutionary code repair agents), which are not cited or compared.
Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned, and the implementation relies on a proprietary backbone with undisclosed agent scaffolding details beyond the prompts.

Writing contains minor issues (e.g., 'Whenever an unexecuted is executed', inconsistent bolding/formatting in tables, Figure 5 legends hard to read), and some claims ('first agent-driven system', 'significantly outperforms in all critical dimensions') are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine gap between zero-shot tool-use/per-sample visual prompt generation and manual, model-specific visual scaffolding, and positions task-wise automated visual prompt discovery as a new paradigm. The declared contribution (Algorithms/General with a systems flavor) is appropriate and the work is judged accordingly.

Technically sensible method design: abstracting the search space from raw code to an 'idea' space directly addresses the long-context distraction problem, and the Novelty-guided UCT with an unexecuted-node prior (Eq. 2) is a reasonable adaptation of UCT to a setting where LLMs can generate unbounded sibling candidates. Semantic backpropagation with sample-wise analysis is a concrete and useful mechanism.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on established perception benchmarks (BlindTest, BLINK) covering accuracy, inference cost, and exploration cost. The comparison to SketchPad+APE under a controlled dev-set protocol is a strong experimental design choice that isolates the benefit of semantic (idea-level) search over text-only prompt optimization (Table 3).

Interesting analysis contributions: the ablation study (Fig. 5) supports each component's necessity, the qualitative examples (Fig. 3) demonstrate genuinely non-obvious discovered strategies (e.g., depth-model repurposing for jigsaw), and the non-transferability analysis (Table 4) provides a memorable, actionable finding that motivates model-specific automated discovery.
Good reproducibility effort: full agent prompts (Appendix A), tool inventory with parameters (Table 1), hyperparameters, and explicit development-set sample indices (Appendix B.3) are provided.
weaknesses: Limited breadth of evaluation: the main results (Tables 2-3) use a single backbone (Gemini-2.5-flash) on only 9 curated tasks with a 30-image development set per task. Given the paper's own claim that visual prompts are model-specific, showing the framework on more backbones (beyond the single-task analysis in Table 4) would substantially strengthen the case. Variance/significance testing is absent for the main results; ablations cover only two tasks.

Potential selection/overfitting concern is not fully resolved: SEVEX selects prompts on a small dev set, and while the SketchPad+APE generalization gap is larger, the paper does not report SEVEX's dev-vs-test gap per task systematically (only aggregate commentary), nor how sensitive the discovered prompt is to the random 30-image dev split.

The self-evaluation scores (s_gain, s_novel) that drive NUCT are produced by the same LLM, introducing a potential self-assessment bias; the paper does not analyze how reliable or calibrated these estimates are, and no sensitivity analysis of the λ hyperparameters is provided.

Novelty is moderate at the component level: tree search with UCT-style selection, feedback-driven idea generation, and insight backpropagation are each well-established ideas; the contribution lies in their combination for this domain rather than a fundamentally new technique. This is acceptable for the declared contribution type but limits theoretical depth (no analysis of NUCT properties).

Fairness of the inference-cost comparisons could be scrutinized: SEVEX's exploration cost (~85k tokens) is an upfront expense only amortized for large test sets, and SketchPad's costs are inflated by full thinking-mode inference, whereas benchmark inference disables thinking for the LVLM — the asymmetric thinking-mode usage deserves clearer justification.

Presentation issues: several typos and broken references (e.g., 'Whenever an unexecuted is executed', the red-colored cross-reference in Fig. 2 caption area, Table 1 reference 'which listed'), and Eq. 2's saturation term direction (penalizing vs. prioritizing) reads ambiguously. These do not undermine the science but should be corrected.

Robustness of discovered prompts over time/model updates is acknowledged only implicitly (Appendix C.1); given rapid LVLM version churn, a brief empirical check of prompt stability across model versions would strengthen the practical significance claims.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper targets automated discovery of task-wise (rather than per-sample) visual prompts for LVLM perception failures, a genuine gap between manual visual scaffolding methods (Viser, BBVPE, Set-of-Mark) and zero-shot tool-use frameworks (Visual SketchPad).

The core methodological idea — searching in an abstract 'idea space' rather than raw code, with novelty-guided UCT selection and semantic backpropagation of sample-wise failure analyses — is sensible and addresses real, articulated challenges (long-context distraction from code, vast unstructured search space).

Broad empirical evidence: 9 tasks across BlindTest and BLINK, three backbones (Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.0), component ablations (abstract space, tree search, semantic backprop), a restricted-toolbox ablation isolating the search contribution from external pretrained tools, and development-split sensitivity analysis — all supporting the claims.

The non-transferability finding (Table 4/Fig. 6) — that visual prompts optimized for one backbone can degrade another — is a valuable, well-documented insight that motivates the entire framework and is useful for the community independently of the method.

Fair-cost reporting: the paper is transparent that SEVEX has a substantial upfront exploration cost (~3,442 naive inferences) and quantifies the break-even point against SketchPad, rather than hiding it. Full agent prompts are included in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
Honest, hedged discussion (Appendix C.2, D) about the scope of the split-stability study and limitations of claims.
weaknesses: The NUCT modification is a heuristic variant of UCT/UCT without theoretical grounding or empirical comparison against the standard UCT baseline in isolation; it is hard to attribute gains to the novelty/saturation terms specifically rather than to the idea-space abstraction or semantic backpropagation. Ablations are only run on two tasks.

Baseline coverage is narrow: the main comparison is against Naive, SketchPad, and SketchPad+APE. Stronger or more natural competitors from LLM-driven program search (e.g., other MCTS/LLM agent optimizers, code-evolution methods) and from automated visual scaffolding are not compared, weakening the claim that SEVEX is the strongest available discovery approach.

Statistical rigor of the main tables is limited: accuracy on the small test sets appears to come from single runs without variance or significance testing; multi-run variance is only reported for CircledLetter in the appendix. Given ~100-sample test sets, several per-task gaps (e.g., Depth, SubwayMap) may not be significant.

Overfitting to the 30-image development set is a real risk, acknowledged but only partially addressed: the split-sensitivity study is limited to a single task, and the dev-test gap for SEVEX is still nonzero and task-dependent (e.g., SemanticCorr dev 72.2 vs test 63.3; SubwayMap 80.0 vs 62.8).

Hyperparameters (λ^expl=0.5, λ^novel=0.15, λ^sat=0.5, k=3, 50 iterations) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, and the self-evaluation scores from the agent that drive unexecuted-node selection are unvalidated — the framework's efficiency could be sensitive to how well the agent calibrates them.
Non-transferability analysis (Table 4) covers only the LineIntersection task with three prompts; generalizing this conclusion across tasks would strengthen the paper's central motivating claim.

Novelty is moderate: the method is a combination of established components (UCT-style tree search, LLM agents, prompt optimization via empirical feedback, failure-driven ideation), and qualitative claims of 'counter-intuitive strategies' rest on a couple of anecdotal examples (Fig. 3).

strengths: The paper addresses a real and relevant problem: automating discovery of task-wise visual prompts for LVLMs, which is currently manual and heuristic. The framing of searching in an abstract 'idea space' rather than raw code is a sensible and well-motivated design choice.

The experimental coverage is reasonably broad for a systems-style contribution: two benchmarks (BlindTest, 5 BLINK tasks), three LVLM backbones (Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.0), component ablations (tree structure, abstract space, semantic backpropagation), a restricted-toolbox ablation (Appendix C.1) that isolates the search contribution from external tools, and a dev-split sensitivity study (Appendix C.2).
The non-transferability analysis (Table 4, Fig. 6) is an interesting and useful empirical finding that supports the motivation for model-specific automated discovery.
Qualitative analyses (Figs. 3, 4, A1) and full prompt listings in the appendix improve transparency of the agentic pipeline.
Inference cost analysis is honest: the paper reports the upfront exploration cost and the break-even point (≈273 SketchPad inferences) rather than only highlighting favorable numbers.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is an LLM-agent pipeline combining well-known ingredients: MCTS/UCT-style tree search, LLM self-evaluation scores, and iterative prompt optimization with empirical feedback (APE [25], OPRO [20], FunSearch/AFlow-style loops). The proposed NUCT is a heuristic variant (max-reward instead of mean, agent-estimated novelty/gain for unexecuted nodes) with no theoretical grounding or analysis of when these heuristics help. For an Algorithms/General contribution, the algorithmic delta over existing agentic search frameworks is incremental.

Overfitting and benchmark-exploitation concerns are not fully resolved. Prompts are optimized on a 30-image dev split and evaluated on the same benchmark's test set. Several tasks show large dev-to-test gaps (SubwayMap 80.0→62.8, SemanticCorr 72.2→63.3, OverlappingShapes 56.7→52.4), and some discovered 'counter-intuitive' strategies (e.g., depth estimation on jigsaw overlays; counting via img1-img2+img3) look like brittle benchmark-specific hacks rather than genuine perceptual improvements. The dev-split sensitivity study covers only one task (CircledLetter) and the authors explicitly do not claim stability elsewhere.

Main results appear to be single runs without variance or significance testing (uncertainty is reported only for the CircledLetter split study). With ~30-image dev sets and modest margins on several tasks (e.g., CircledLetter 83.7 vs SketchPad 82.0; Depth ties at 85.1), the claimed superiority is not statistically established. Ablations are also limited to two tasks for resource reasons.

Baseline coverage is narrow. The only exploration-based comparison is SketchPad+APE. No comparison against direct search over visual prompts without the idea abstraction (e.g., code-level evolution, OPRO on code, other agentic search systems), which is exactly what is needed to validate the central 'semantic abstraction' claim beyond the w/o-abstract-space ablation on two tasks.

Some methodological details are unclear or raise fairness questions. It is not fully explained how the discovered code is handled at inference time such that inference cost is near-naive (is the code pre-executed/cached per image class?); the 'thinking' feature is disabled for baselines' benchmark inference but enabled for SEVEX's agent stages; SketchPad was modified by adding tools, complicating comparison to its published results; hyperparameters (λ_expl=0.5, λ_novel=0.15, λ_sat=0.5, k=3, 50 iterations) are fixed without any sensitivity analysis.

Self-evaluated scores (s_gain, s_novel, feasibility) come from the same LLM that generates the ideas, introducing correlated bias in node selection that the paper neither measures nor mitigates (e.g., no calibration analysis of these scores against realized rewards).
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, despite the framework's heavy dependence on prompts, tool lists, and stochastic agent behavior.

Presentation issues: some claims are overstated relative to evidence ('significantly outperforms', 'new paradigm'), the related-work positioning ('previous methods... relied on manual human trial-and-error') glosses over existing automated search approaches, and there are grammatical/editorial slips (e.g., 'experiments the visual prompt', D.3).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: automating the discovery of task-wise (rather than per-sample) visual prompts for LVLMs, positioned clearly against tool-use paradigms (e.g., SketchPad) and text-only prompt optimization (APE). The idea-space abstraction that decouples semantic intent from code implementation is a sensible and well-motivated design choice that directly targets the stated low-code-distraction and search-space challenges.

The experimental evaluation is broad for this type of work: comparisons on nine tasks across two perception-focused benchmarks (BlindTest, BLINK), generality tests on three LVLM backbones (Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.0), an ablation of the exploration components (tree structure, semantic backpropagation, abstract space), a restricted-toolbox ablation (Appendix C.1), and a development-split sensitivity study (Appendix C.2). The non-transferability analysis (Table 4) is an interesting and practically important finding that motivates the entire framework.

The efficiency claims are well supported quantitatively: inference cost is amortized (only ~10.9% over Naive vs. ~10x for SketchPad), and exploration cost is ~11.5% of SketchPad+APE, with a concrete break-even analysis (273 SketchPad inferences).

The qualitative results (Figure 3) demonstrate genuinely emergent, counter-intuitive strategies (e.g., using a depth-estimation model to detect jigsaw discontinuities), which supports the claim that the framework goes beyond human-biased tool usage.

Reproducibility support is good: all agent prompts are included in the appendix, the visual tool inventory is fully specified (Table 1), hyperparameters and dev-set indices are disclosed, and limitations are honestly scoped (e.g., the authors explicitly do not claim split stability for all tasks).
weaknesses: Statistical rigor of the main results is limited: Table 2 and Table 3 report single-run accuracies without variance or confidence intervals, despite using a small 30-image development set and a stochastic, LLM-driven search. The stability claims in Section 4.2 and Appendix C.2 rest on only two additional splits of a single task (CircledLetter); the significant dev-to-test gaps in some tasks (e.g., SubwayMap: 80.0 dev vs. 62.8 test) suggest some residual overfitting that deserves broader analysis.

The baseline set is narrow. The main comparison is against Naive, SketchPad, and SketchPad+APE. There is no comparison to other agentic search or LLM-based optimization frameworks (e.g., other tree-search-with-LLM pipelines, OPRO-style optimizers adapted to visual prompts), and no human-expert manual prompt engineering baseline, even though the core motivation is replacing manual trial-and-error; a small human baseline would substantially strengthen the central claim.

Several methodological details are under-specified or appear ad hoc: the novelty-guided UCT (NUCT) formulas are plausible but not theoretically analyzed, the hyperparameters (λ^expl=0.5, λ^novel=0.15, λ^sat=0.5, k=3) are reported without sensitivity analysis, and how the Analyst agent's 'actionable insights' interact with the numeric reward (and whether insights can mislead the search) is not examined.

External pre-trained tools (GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, DepthAnything) play a role in the headline results; although the restricted-toolbox ablation (Table A1) is appreciated and shows most gains persist, it covers only the four BlindTest tasks, leaving the contribution of external tools on BLINK tasks (e.g., Jigsaw, where the flagship counter-intuitive result relies on DepthAnything) unquantified.

Task coverage is limited to nine tasks drawn largely from synthetic/controlled benchmarks (BlindTest plus five BLINK tasks following SketchPad's protocol), so the generalization of 'task-wise visual prompt discovery' to natural, real-world visual tasks remains untested.

Minor presentation issues: some terminology and figure notation (e.g., reward definitions, normalization of self-evaluation scores) require careful reading, and the borderline formatting/typos in Figure 6 and Appendix text slightly reduce polish.
